name: David Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo at Marlow Deep, which is an underground gold mine outside Brennick. A jumbo is a drill rig with two big arms, and my job is drilling the face so the charge-up crew can blast the next three and a half metres of tunnel. I lead the development crew on day shift, four of us. The best bit is when you mark up a face, drill sixty holes, and the blast pulls clean, square walls, no mess. The worst is heat at level 14, it's 34 degrees down there before you turn anything on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside of work, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Me and Noor live in a rented two-bedroom on Station Street, she's a nurse at the district hospital. Money's tight, though. Marlow pays less than the big mines out west, and since my dad's knee surgery I've been covering half his rent, so we've got maybe three weeks of savings. There's one other mine within driving distance and it's not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly that sounds like most new things at work. Big launch, a few emails, then back to normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about the stuff that actually matters, like ventilation on level 14 and the pay gap with the western mines. I'd probably make a joke in the crib room that the robot apocalypse got cancelled. Crib room is our lunch room, by the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but it also means nothing gets fixed by magic. I'd still be on low pay, still helping Dad, still one bad month from a credit card. The plateau doesn't fix the stuff that's already wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and push the union on the pay gap, because that's the real issue in this picture. I'd keep using the AI thing on my phone now and then for writing up incident reports, it saves me twenty minutes. And I'd try to get a month's buffer by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, like hearing the weather will be the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI for incident reports. What's that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's handy. I talk into it what happened, a hose blew on the boom or whatever, and it turns it into the format the safety office wants. I check it, because once it wrote that the hose was replaced when it wasn't. So it's a tool, like a torque wrench, not a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the month's buffer come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overtime mostly, Saturdays on the rehab crew. And cooking at home, Noor's been on at me to stop buying petrol station pies. It's not glamorous, but three Saturdays gets me most of the way.

S0.say: Good, now we can talk about what matters, like ventilation on level 14 and the pay gap with the western mines. I'd joke in the lunch room that the robot apocalypse got cancelled.
S0.think: It's a relief, but nothing gets fixed by magic. I'd still be on low pay, still helping Dad, and still one bad month from a credit card.
S0.do: Keeps working as he is, presses the union on the pay gap, and keeps using an AI app now and then to write up incident reports. Works Saturday overtime to build a month's buffer by Christmas.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a forecast that says same as yesterday.
S0.quote: So it's a tool, like a torque wrench, not a person.
S0.fieldNote: David already uses AI casually and checks its work, which gives him a grounded view. He turns the calm picture straight to the problems that already exist: pay, heat and his father's rent. He sounds practical rather than angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can see. We've already got a jumbo upstairs that drills a pattern on its own if you set it up right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to get ahead of it, not fight it after the fact. I'd say it at the meeting: we want first go at the new jobs, paid training, and no one pushed out without a real offer. I'd share that on the members' group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be okay, because I'm good with the rigs and I pick things up once I see them working. The guys I'd worry about are the ones who only know one way. But okay isn't great, I'd still be on the same low money doing a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the automated jumbo was proven on another crew, I'd put my hand up for the training, maybe in the first six months. I'd ask the union to get the rate for the remote operator role written down before anyone signs up. And I'd keep the Saturday overtime so I've got a cushion if the shifts change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I guess. Not scared, but I'd be watching closely, like when the roof starts talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, when the roof starts talking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Underground, the rock makes little cracking noises before it moves. Most of the time it's nothing. But you never stop listening, and that's what this would feel like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gaz, my drill partner, he's 41 and he's brilliant on the gear but he hates screens. I'd want to sit with him and show him the controls on breaks. If the union gets paid training, I'd make sure he's on the list.

S1.say: The union needs to get ahead of it, not fight it after. We want first go at the new jobs, paid training, and nobody pushed out without a real offer.
S1.think: I'd probably be okay because I'm good with the rigs and learn once I see something work. But okay isn't great: same low money, different job, and I'd worry for the ones who know only one way.
S1.do: Volunteers for training on the automated drill rig within six months once it is proven on another crew. Asks the union to fix the remote operator's pay rate in writing first, and keeps Saturday overtime as a cushion.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, like listening to the roof crack underground.
S1.quote: Most of the time it's nothing. But you never stop listening, and that's what this would feel like.
S1.fieldNote: He waits for proof, then moves, which is exactly how he describes himself. His instinct is to bring colleagues along, especially Gaz. He wants the union to set terms before change, not resist it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's not change, that's the floor dropping out. Wow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that the companies should be made to share it. If a robot does my job for a third of the cost, some of that saving should go to the people who used to do it. I'd be on the members' group every night, and I'd go to the protest in the capital if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be really frightened. Underground is where robots make the most sense, because no one wants people down there in the heat anyway. With three weeks of savings and Dad's rent, I don't know how we'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop covering Dad's rent and ask my sister to take a turn, which would be an awful conversation. I'd sell the pickup and buy something cheap, which frees up four hundred a month. Noor's job is probably safer than mine for a bit, so we'd live off her pay while I looked for anything, and I'd push the union for a big payout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight just thinking about it. Two years is nothing when you've got nothing behind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. Two years is barely enough to finish a course, so there's no point retraining into something the AI also does by 2028. All I can do is cut back and lean on Noor. I hate that, but that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd live off Noor's pay. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say of course, she's like that. But I'd feel like I'd failed her. My dad worked thirty years and never once lived off my mum's pay, and I know it's old-fashioned, but it'd sting.

S2.say: Companies should be made to share it: if a robot does my job for a third of the cost, some of that saving should go to the people who did it. I'd be at the protest in the capital.
S2.think: I'd be really frightened, because underground is where robots make the most sense. With three weeks of savings and Dad's rent, I don't know how we'd manage.
S2.do: Stops covering his father's rent, asks his sister to take a turn, and sells his pickup for a cheaper car to save four hundred a month. Lives off his partner's nursing pay while job hunting and pushes the union for a large payout.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a tight chest; two years is nothing with no savings behind him.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when you've got nothing behind you.
S2.fieldNote: His progressive line about sharing gains is sincere, but his private fear is about the household budget. He admits feeling he'd fail his partner by relying on her pay, a more traditional feeling than his politics suggest. The short warning time rules out retraining for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough to get my head around, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set up proper retraining and a wage guarantee, so let's not waste the first two arguing. I'd say it to the union and to our member of parliament. Five years is one election cycle and a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I've got maybe three years left at Marlow, because they'd start replacing the jumbos before 2031. I'd want to be out and into something else before the queue forms. The question is what, because I'm not sure anything is safe in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd start an electrical apprenticeship, part-time, through the mine's own training program while it still exists. Electricians will be needed to put all these machines in, at least for a while. I'd keep Saturdays, cut the takeaway, and try to get two months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a busy kind of anxious. Like having a deadline instead of a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing is safe in this picture. Why the electrical apprenticeship, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to wire the robots in and fix them while everyone's still working it out. Maybe that's five good years, maybe ten. It's not forever, I know that, but it's better than being the last guy on the jumbo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me a ticket, a qualification I can take anywhere. With two years I'd just be cutting back. With five I can actually get somewhere before it lands, and I'd still be 32, so not too late.

S3.say: We've got five years to set up retraining and a wage guarantee, so let's not waste two arguing. I'd say it to the union and our member of parliament.
S3.think: I've probably got three years left at the mine before the jumbos go. I want to be out before the queue forms, but I'm not sure anything is safe.
S3.do: Starts a part-time electrical apprenticeship through the mine's training program in year one. Keeps Saturday overtime and cuts takeaway to reach two months of savings.
S3.feel: Anxious, but a busy kind of anxious, like a deadline rather than a disaster.
S3.quote: Like having a deadline instead of a disaster.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns David from cutting back to building a qualification. He's clear-eyed that electrical work may only last a while, but sees it as a better bet than staying. He keeps tying change to political timelines like elections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." What goes through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. I'd be 37. Kids, maybe, by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. Ten years is long enough to train a whole generation of miners for something else. If governments and companies mess this one up, it's on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be alright in this one. I'd do the electrical ticket, then maybe automation tech, and keep moving one step ahead. What worries me is Noor and me wanting kids around 30, and doing that while I'm halfway through retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling for a couple more years and start the electrical apprenticeship around year two, once the first automated rigs show up. I'd save a little each month instead of all at once. And I'd sit down with Noor and actually plan when we'd try for a baby, around my study, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the others. It's like knowing a mine will close in ten years. Sad, but you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a couple of years before starting the apprenticeship. Why not start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in ten years I'd want to see which way it goes first. That's how I am, I'm not the first one to try the new rig, I'm the second. Waiting a bit means I pick the right ticket, not just the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gaz in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to come with me, do the course. He'd say he's too old, and I'd say you'll be 51, that's not old. Ten years is enough for even Gaz to learn a screen.

S4.say: This is the version where nobody should be left behind. Ten years is long enough to retrain a whole generation of miners, so if it goes wrong, it's on purpose.
S4.think: I'd be alright in this one, doing the electrical ticket then maybe automation tech. My worry is planning kids with Noor around 30 while halfway through retraining.
S4.do: Keeps drilling for two years, then starts the electrical apprenticeship once the first automated rigs appear. Saves steadily and plans with his partner to time having a baby around his study.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like knowing a mine closes in ten years and planning around it.
S4.quote: I'm not the first one to try the new rig, I'm the second.
S4.fieldNote: His steady nature shows clearly: with a decade, he'd deliberately wait to see which training pays off. Family plans come into view only in this picture. He keeps returning to bringing Gaz along.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a guaranteed income for a couple of years while people retrain, paid for by the companies that use the robots. And free courses at the college, not ones where you pay three grand and hope.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the heat. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody mentions that some of these jobs are bad for your body. If a robot drills level 14 in 34 degrees, part of me says good. I just want to still be able to pay rent when it does.

headlineQuote: If a robot drills level 14 in 34 degrees, part of me says good. I just want to still be able to pay rent when it does.
portrait: David Khan is a 27-year-old development drill-rig lead at an underground gold mine, living with his nurse partner Noor and covering half his father's rent on below-average pay. He uses AI now and then for incident reports and treats it like any tool, checking its work. He's calm in the plateau picture and uneasy but ready to train once automation is proven. Two-year AGI alarms him and pushes him to lean on Noor's pay, which stings, while five and ten years let him plan an electrical apprenticeship and even family timing. He wants unions and government to make the companies share the savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because with three weeks of savings and family to support there'd be no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a couple of years while people retrain, paid by the companies using robots, and free courses at the local college.
